newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Metals - Aluminium squeeze said under way.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - Aluminium squeeze said under way.

text.p: Aluminium appears to be in the cross-hairs of a speculative squeeze only days after zinc was pounded earlier this week, base metal dealers said on Friday.

Talk that a squeeze is under way has been fuelled by the recent rise in aluminium prices to five month highs on the London Metal Exchange (LME) while global consumer demand remains stagnant, they added.
Prices on the LME rose on Thursday to a late quote of US$1,712/15 a tonne compared with about $1,550 three months ago.

Despite flat demand, LME stocks have dropped sharply to 627,125 tonnes on Thursday from 800,475 a tonnes at the end of April. The market has also lapsed into backwardation, indicating nearby physical tightness, when it was in contango last week.
"It's an artificial squeeze," a veteran aluminium dealer told Reuters. "Aside from the long-term contracts, spot business has died down quite a bit."

"Consumers in the U.S. would like to take more, but the price is too high. Europe is dead in July and August. Chinese demand is flat and almost nothing is happening in Asia. Where is the demand coming from to justify the fall in stocks?"
Other traders were more cautious, but concede the current price does not seem to be supported by fundamentals.
"Business is very slow, especially here in Asia. It's almost nominal. But it's very difficult to say if there is a squeeze underway in the market," a Japanese dealer said.
Brokers Macquarie said in its daily review the targets of the squeeze are believed to be traders who hold large volumes of uncovered call options at $1,700 a tonne.
"The main tightness appears to be centred around the August prompt date and again in November," Macquarie said.
The critical question, however, for a squeeze to be successful would be if the market is sufficiently tight and whether the shorts can cover their positions.
The level of market stocks and the control of those stocks would therefore be vital, traders and analysts said.

An aluminium dealer in Singapore said a U.S. investment house and a British metal company with links to a major bank control most of the 500,000 to one million tonnes of aluminium lying in "hidden" or unreported stocks of the metal.

"These two have the financial power to finance these hidden stocks. They're holding the longs in the market. If you look behind the curtain and you see the hidden stocks and the new capacity coming on, you have to ask why are prices at these levels?" he said.

"These stocks have been financed by banks using the contango. With the market having swung into backwardation, refinancing of stocks is no longer possible," Macquarie said. "Without control of this material, prospects of a successful squeeze are poor."
Another dealer said the market is wondering when the warrants on the hidden stocks of aluminium come due.
"When is the deadline for these warrants? If they see the contango has practically disappeared, the stocks will have to be released to the LME," he said.
The only fly in the ointment of a squeeze would be if higher prices prompts the restart of idled capacity which is currently estimated at 780,000 tonnes a year.
But Alcoa of Australia Ltd on Thursday denied rumours it is planning to restart any of its idled capacity.
One dealer said the fund-driven surge in aluminium prices may end soon if the British and American firm decide to liquidate their position and take their profits.
"If the signal comes to sell, they can start liquidating like hell and go into something like pork bellies," he said. "The funds are the driving force in commodities now. It's no longer predictable."
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
